title: Gerund and Infinitive Verbs
summary: Which English verbs are followed by -ing, which need to + verb, and which accept both.

lessons.title: Verbs Followed by -ing
lessons.summary: The verb + -ing pattern and the verbs that never take to.

steps.heading: Verb + -ing
steps.body: A large group of English verbs cannot be followed by to + verb. Instead they need the -ing form, called the gerund. These verbs usually describe something pleasant or unpleasant that is merely the activity itself, not a planned result. The most reliable way to learn them is in groups, because the same handful accounts for almost all mistakes.

rules.title: The pattern
rules.statement: After these verbs the verb takes the -ing form and never the to-infinitive. The subject of the -ing clause is normally the same as the subject of the main verb.

examples.en: She enjoys reading before bed.
examples.vi: Cô ấy thích đọc sách trước khi ngủ.
examples.note: enjoy + reading, not enjoy to read

examples.en: I don't mind waiting a little longer.
examples.vi: Tôi không ngại chờ thêm một chút.

rules.title: Common verb groups
rules.statement: The verbs are easiest to remember in clusters: enjoyment, evaluation, avoidance and thought.
rules.formula: enjoy, like, dislike, love, hate, prefer, mind | finish, quit, suggest, consider, imagine, risk, avoid, deny, admit, delay | keep, practise, miss, waste, admit

examples.en: He finished reading the book last week.
examples.vi: Anh ấy đã đọc xong cuốn sách tuần trước.

examples.en: They postponed having the meeting.
examples.vi: Họ đã hoãn việc họp lại.

rules.title: Prepositions also take -ing
rules.statement: After a preposition the verb always takes the -ing form, with no exception, whatever the main verb is.

examples.en: I'm looking forward to seeing you again.
examples.vi: Tôi rất mong được gặp lại bạn.
examples.note: to here is a preposition, not an infinitive

examples.en: She is good at solving difficult problems.
examples.vi: Cô ấy giỏi giải quyết những vấn đề khó.

examples.en: I really enjoy learning new languages.
examples.vi: Tôi thật sự thích học ngôn ngữ mới.

examples.en: Have you ever tried riding a motorbike?
examples.vi: Bạn đã bao giờ thử đi xe máy chưa?

examples.en: He denied taking the money.
examples.vi: Anh ấy đã phủ nhận việc lấy tiền.
examples.note: deny + -ing; the gerund names the accusation

examples.en: They suggested meeting at seven.
examples.vi: Họ gợi ý họp lúc bảy giờ.
examples.note: suggest + -ing, with the meeting as the topic

examples.en: Stop worrying about the exam.
examples.vi: Đừng lo lắng về kỳ thi nữa.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.

items.text: She suggested to meet at eight.

exercises.explanation: Suggest is one of the verbs that only takes the -ing form, so suggested meeting is the only option. Learners who answer a reach for the to-infinitive because the English word suggest looks like a verb of planning; the reason is that suggest is about mentioning a topic, not making a decision.

exercises.prompt: We have finished ___ (pack) our bags.
exercises.explanation: Finish is followed by the -ing form: packing. The only other candidate, packed, is a past participle, and the pattern here is verb + gerund, not have + participle.

exercises.prompt: I am looking forward to meet my cousin next week.

values: I am looking forward to meeting my cousin next week.

exercises.explanation: In look forward to, the to is a preposition, and a preposition is always followed by the -ing form. Writing to meet treats the preposition as the start of an infinitive, which is the standard error in this pattern.

exercises.prompt: Match each verb to the form it takes.
exercises.instruction: Pair every verb with the correct pattern.
exercises.explanation: All four verbs in this set take only the -ing form, which is why they are grouped together in the first place. Recognising a cluster makes the pattern predictable instead of something to be checked verb by verb.

audio.text: She denied taking the last slice of cake.

acceptedAnswers: She denied taking the last slice of cake.
items.translation: Cô ấy phủ nhận việc đã ăn miếng bánh cuối cùng.

audio.text: I am looking forward to hearing from you soon.

acceptedAnswers: I am looking forward to hearing from you soon.
items.hint: to is a preposition, so use -ing
items.translation: Tôi mong sớm được tin từ bạn.

items.text: He avoids to pay the fees in advance.
He avoids paying the fees in advance.
He avoids pay the fees in advance.
He avoids paid the fees in advance.

questions.explanation: Avoid is followed by the gerund only: avoids paying. Option c uses a bare base verb and option d uses the past participle, and neither can follow avoid in English.

questions.prompt: Write the -ing form of the verb 'to travel'.
questions.explanation: The -ing form of travel is travelling, with the final consonant doubled because the stress falls on the second syllable. American spelling drops the second l, so both variants are accepted here.

questions.prompt: He is good at play chess.

values: He is good at playing chess.

questions.explanation: After the preposition at the verb must be in the -ing form: playing. There is no exception for short verbs, and no to-infinitive is possible after a preposition.

takeaways: A large group of English verbs takes only the -ing form: enjoy, mind, finish, suggest, avoid.
After any preposition the verb must be in the -ing form.
In look forward to and be used to, the to is a preposition, so the gerund follows.
The gerund usually shares the subject of the main verb: She enjoys reading.

lessons.title: Verbs Followed by to + Verb
lessons.summary: The to-infinitive pattern, and how it differs from the gerund.

steps.heading: Verb + to + Verb
steps.body: The to-infinitive is the opposite cluster: these verbs are about intention, decision, promise and attempt, and they cannot be followed by -ing. A useful contrast with the gerund verbs is that the -ing group describes the activity itself, while the to-infinitive group describes what someone intends or tries to do. The two groups are almost complementary, so learning them side by side is much faster than learning them one by one.

rules.title: The pattern
rules.statement: After these verbs, put to + base form of the next verb. The to may be dropped only after a modal or another auxiliary.

examples.en: I want to learn Japanese.
examples.vi: Tôi muốn học tiếng Nhật.

examples.en: She decided to move abroad.
examples.vi: Cô ấy quyết định đi nước ngoài.

rules.title: Common verb groups
rules.statement: Group them by meaning: intention, decision and obligation, effort and judgement.
rules.formula: want, hope, plan, intend, would like, offer | decide, agree, promise, refuse, manage | try, attempt, learn, manage | pretend, seem, appear, claim

examples.en: He refused to pay the fine.
examples.vi: Anh ấy từ chối nộp phạt.

examples.en: They agreed to meet earlier.
examples.vi: Họ đồng ý gặp sớm hơn.

rules.title: After modals and auxiliaries
rules.statement: Modals and auxiliaries are followed by the bare base form, with no to at all.
rules.formula: can / will / must / should / would + base verb

examples.en: I can help you with that.
examples.vi: Tôi có thể giúp bạn việc đó.
examples.note: can + help, not can to help

examples.en: You should book the tickets early.
examples.vi: Bạn nên đặt vé sớm.

examples.en: My parents hope to visit me next year.
examples.vi: Bố mẹ tôi hy vọng được thăm tôi vào năm sau.

examples.en: He learned to swim when he was six.
examples.vi: Anh ấy học bơi khi sáu tuổi.
examples.note: learn + to + base verb: skill acquired

examples.en: I would like to book a window seat.
examples.vi: Tôi muốn đặt một ghế cạnh cửa sổ.
examples.note: would like + to + base verb, polite

examples.en: They pretended to understand the question.
examples.vi: Họ giả vờ hiểu câu hỏi.

examples.en: I don't want to argue about it now.
examples.vi: Tôi không muốn tranh luận về chuyện đó bây giờ.
examples.note: negative: do not + want + to + base verb

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.

items.text: I am wanting to learn Spanish.

exercises.explanation: Want belongs to the to-infinitive group, so want to learn is correct. Option a uses the gerund, which belongs to verbs such as enjoy and avoid; option c leaves out the to; option d adds an auxiliary that want does not need.

exercises.prompt: They agreed ___ (meet) in front of the library.
exercises.explanation: Agree is followed by to + base verb, so to meet is required. Agree is a good example of a verb that is easy to confuse with enjoy-type verbs, because the two groups differ only in the pattern, not in the meaning of the English word.

exercises.prompt: She refused paying for the meal.

values: She refused to pay for the meal.

exercises.explanation: Refuse takes the to-infinitive, so both the pattern and the verb form change: refused to pay. Paying is a gerund, which is what would be required after a verb like enjoy, not after refuse.

exercises.prompt: Match each verb to the pattern it takes.
exercises.instruction: Pair every verb with the correct pattern.
exercises.explanation: Hope, manage, promise and refuse all belong to the to-infinitive group. Notice that refuse is the opposite of enjoy in meaning but opposite in pattern too, which is exactly why the two sets have to be learned separately.

audio.text: I would like to reserve a table for two people.

acceptedAnswers: I would like to reserve a table for two people.
items.translation: Tôi muốn đặt bàn cho hai người.

audio.text: They promised to send the documents before Friday.

acceptedAnswers: They promised to send the documents before Friday.
items.translation: Họ hứa sẽ gửi giấy tờ trước thứ Sáu.

items.text: She promised to be there at six.
She promised being there at six.
She promised to being there at six.
She promised that there at six.

questions.explanation: After to we need the base form: to be. Option b uses the gerund, and option c stacks an -ing form onto the infinitive; the two patterns are alternatives, never a combination.

questions.prompt: I can to help you with your English.

values: I can help you with your English.

questions.explanation: After a modal, English uses the bare base form with no to at all: can help. The to-infinitive is for ordinary verbs such as want and decide, and modals are the exception to that pattern.

questions.prompt: Write the -ing form of the verb 'to run'.
questions.explanation: Run doubles its final consonant before -ing because the stress falls on the last syllable: running. This matters when you see running in a gerund pattern, as in She enjoys running every morning.

takeaways: Verbs of intention, decision, promise and effort take to + base verb.
want, hope, plan, decide, agree, promise, refuse, offer and manage all follow this pattern.
After a modal or auxiliary, the to disappears: can help, will book, must be.
The to-infinitive and the gerund are alternatives; never mix them in one phrase.

lessons.title: Verbs That Take Both
lessons.summary: remember, forget, stop, try, regret and mean change meaning with the form.

steps.heading: Two Patterns, Two Meanings
steps.body: A small group of verbs accepts both the gerund and the to-infinitive, and the choice changes the meaning rather than the grammar. With the gerund the verb looks back at something that already happened; with the to-infinitive it looks forward at something not yet done. Learning these verbs in pairs is the only reliable way to control the difference.

rules.title: Remember and forget
rules.statement: The gerund refers to a past action you recall; the to-infinitive refers to a future action you must not forget.
rules.formula: remember doing = recall the past | remember to do = not forget

examples.en: I remember locking the door.
examples.vi: Tôi nhớ là đã khóa cửa.
examples.note: gerund: the action is a memory

examples.en: Remember to lock the door when you leave.
examples.vi: Nhớ khóa cửa khi bạn ra đi.
examples.note: infinitive: an instruction for the future

rules.title: Stop and try
rules.statement: After stop the gerund means quit the activity; the infinitive means prevent it. After try the gerund means experiment; the infinitive means attempt.
rules.formula: stop doing = quit | stop to do = pause in order to do | try doing = experiment | try to do = attempt

examples.en: He stopped smoking last year.
examples.vi: Anh ấy đã bỏ thuốc lá năm ngoái.

examples.en: She stopped to smoke at the corner.
examples.vi: Cô ấy dừng lại để hút thuốc ở góc phố.
examples.note: stop + to: she paused for another purpose

rules.title: Regret and mean
rules.statement: Regret doing looks back with sorry; regret to do apologises now for something ahead. Mean doing refers to what something signifies; mean to do refers to intention.
rules.formula: regret doing = sorry about the past | regret to do = apologise now | mean doing = signify | mean to do = intend

examples.en: I regret telling her the truth.
examples.vi: Tôi hối hận vì đã nói thật với cô ấy.
examples.note: gerund: the telling is already done

examples.en: I regret to inform you that your application was rejected.
examples.vi: Tôi rất tiếc phải thông báo rằng hồ sơ của bạn đã bị từ chối.
examples.note: infinitive: the rejection is the news being given now

examples.en: Don't forget to bring your passport.
examples.vi: Đừng quên mang hộ chiếu theo.

examples.en: I'll never forget meeting her at that conference.
examples.vi: Tôi sẽ không bao giờ quên cuộc gặp gỡ cô ấy tại hội nghị đó.
examples.note: gerund: a memory of the past

examples.en: He tried to lift the box but it was too heavy.
examples.vi: Anh ấy cố bê chiếc hộp nhưng nó quá nặng.
examples.note: try + to: an attempt at a task

examples.en: We tried living in the countryside for a month.
examples.vi: Chúng tôi đã thử sống ở nông thôn trong một tháng.

examples.en: What do you mean by saying that?
examples.vi: Bạn nói vậy nghĩa là gì?

exercises.prompt: You are about to leave the office. Which sentence is right?
exercises.explanation: The action has not happened yet, so remember to lock is the instruction. Remember locking would only make sense if you were looking back at a past action, and option c mixes the two patterns in a way English does not allow.

exercises.prompt: Which sentences describe something that already happened? Select all that apply.
exercises.explanation: The gerund points back at a past event, so remember meeting and stopped smoking both describe what has already happened. The to-infinitive points forward: remember to meet is a future reminder and stopped to smoke means he paused in order to smoke.

exercises.prompt: I regret to lose my passport on the trip.
exercises.instruction: Rewrite the sentence so that it refers to what has already happened.

values: I regret losing my passport on the trip.

exercises.explanation: Losing the passport is already past, so the gerund is correct: regret losing. Regret to do is reserved for apologising now about news you are about to deliver, as in I regret to inform you.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the correct form: 'She stopped ___ when the alarm rang.'
exercises.explanation: An alarm ringing is a sudden interruption of an activity already in progress, so the background action is a gerund: stopped smoking. If the intended meaning were that she paused in order to do something, the sentence would need a different structure such as She stopped to smoke.

audio.text: I will never forget taking that first flight.

acceptedAnswers: I will never forget taking that first flight.
items.hint: forget + -ing looks back at the past
items.translation: Tôi sẽ không bao giờ quên chuyến bay đầu tiên đó.

audio.text: He stopped to buy some fruit on the way home.

acceptedAnswers: He stopped to buy some fruit on the way home.
items.hint: stop + to = pause in order to do something
items.translation: Anh ấy dừng lại mua trái cây trên đường về nhà.

questions.explanation: Stopping the activity itself is stop plus the gerund: stopped smoking. Option b means he paused his journey in order to have a cigarette, which is the opposite life choice.

questions.prompt: He suggested to meet at the airport.

values: He suggested meeting at the airport.

questions.explanation: Suggest never takes a to-infinitive, so the correct form is suggested meeting. This is the most common error in the whole area, and it happens because suggested is often confused with advised or proposed, which do take the infinitive.

questions.prompt: Write the -ing form of the verb 'to mean'.
questions.explanation: Mean takes the -ing form without changing its spelling: meaning, as in I don't know what you're meaning by that. Written as meanning it would be a spelling error, since a stressed long vowel does not double the consonant.

takeaways: remember, forget, stop, try, regret and mean accept both patterns.
The gerund looks back at what has already happened; the infinitive looks forward.
stop doing means quit; stop to do means pause in order to do something else.
try doing means experiment; try to do means attempt a task.

lessons.title: Form and Meaning Shifts
lessons.summary: Prepositions that look like infinitives, and patterns that change meaning with the form.

steps.heading: Prepositions, Adjectives and Meaning Shifts
steps.body: Several English patterns look like infinitives but are not, and the grammar only makes sense once you can tell them apart. The verb phrase be used to is the classic trap: used to is the past habit marker, while be used to is a passive meaning accustomed, followed by a noun or a gerund. Adjective patterns such as be interested in work the same way, with a preposition plus gerund.

rules.title: Used to and be used to
rules.statement: Used to + base verb describes a habit that has stopped. Be used to + noun or gerund describes a habit that still holds.
rules.formula: used to + base verb (past habit) | be used to + noun / -ing (accustomed)

examples.en: I used to work at night.
examples.vi: Trước đây tôi từng làm việc vào ban đêm.
examples.note: past habit that no longer applies

examples.en: I am used to working at night.
examples.vi: Tôi đã quen làm việc vào ban đêm.

rules.title: Preposition plus gerund after adjectives
rules.statement: A group of adjectives takes a fixed preposition, and the verb after it is always in the -ing form.
rules.formula: interested in, keen on, good at, bad at, surprised at, worried about

examples.en: She is interested in learning Korean.
examples.vi: Cô ấy quan tâm đến việc học tiếng Hàn.

examples.en: I am worried about missing the deadline.
examples.vi: Tôi lo lắng về việc sẽ hết hạn.

rules.title: Verbs whose meaning changes
rules.statement: A few verbs differ more than a glance between the two patterns: prefer doing means enjoying something generally, while prefer to do means choosing one option.
rules.formula: I prefer walking. / I prefer to walk.

examples.en: I prefer reading to watching television.
examples.vi: Tôi thích đọc sách hơn là xem tivi.

examples.en: I prefer to walk rather than take the bus.
examples.vi: Tôi thà đi bộ còn hơn đi xe buýt.
examples.note: a choice between two specific options

examples.en: He used to smoke, but he stopped two years ago.
examples.vi: Trước đây anh ấy từng hút thuốc, nhưng hai năm trước anh ấy đã bỏ.
examples.note: used to marks a habit that has ended

examples.en: I'm not used to getting up so early.
examples.vi: Tôi không quen dậy sớm như vậy.
examples.note: be used to = accustomed, so gerund follows

examples.en: They are keen on joining the marathon.
examples.vi: Họ rất háo hức tham gia marathon.

examples.en: He was surprised to see the changes.
examples.vi: Anh ấy đã rất ngạc nhiên khi thấy những thay đổi.
examples.note: surprised to see, a to-infinitive after an adjective

examples.en: I prefer to take the train on long journeys.
examples.vi: Tôi thà đi tàu hơn trên những chuyến đi dài.
examples.note: prefer to do for a specific choice

exercises.prompt: Choose the sentence that means 'he is accustomed to working at night'.

items.text: He used to work at night.
He is used to working at night.
He is used to work at night.
He is use to working at night.

exercises.explanation: Be used to is the passive meaning accustomed, so it is followed by a gerund. Option a describes a habit that has stopped, option c wrongly puts a base verb after the adjective phrase, and option d gets the spelling of the passive participle wrong.

exercises.prompt: She is interested in to study history.

values: She is interested in studying history.

exercises.explanation: In interested in, the in is a preposition, and prepositions are followed by the gerund: studying. This is the general rule that fixes the whole family of patterns, including keen on and good at.

exercises.prompt: The phrase 'used to' followed by a base verb describes a habit in the past that no longer continues.
exercises.instruction: Decide whether the statement is true or false.
exercises.explanation: The statement is true. Used to plus a base verb is the past habit marker and always implies the habit has ended, which is why speakers add a negation when they want to keep it: I used to not like coffee.

exercises.prompt: I am not used to ___ (get) up at five in the morning.
exercises.explanation: After be used to the verb takes the -ing form, so getting is required. Using the bare form get is the classic confusion between the habit marker used to and the adjective be used to.

audio.text: I am used to getting up early, but my sister is not.

acceptedAnswers: I am used to getting up early, but my sister is not.
items.translation: Tôi quen dậy sớm, nhưng em gái tôi thì không.

audio.text: She is keen on taking part in the debate club.

acceptedAnswers: She is keen on taking part in the debate club.
items.translation: Cô ấy rất háo hức tham gia câu lạc bộ tranh luận.

questions.prompt: He is used to work in the morning now.

values: He is used to working in the morning now.

questions.explanation: Be used to here means accustomed, so the following verb must be the gerund working. If the intended meaning were the past habit that has stopped, the sentence would be He used to work in the morning.

questions.prompt: Which pattern is correct after the adjective 'interested'?
questions.explanation: Interested takes the preposition in, and a preposition is followed by the gerund: interested in learning. Be interested to do is a common but incorrect mixture of the two patterns.

questions.prompt: Write the -ing form of the verb 'to prefer'.
questions.explanation: Prefer doubles the r before -ing: preferring, because the stress falls on the second syllable. Both prefer + -ing and prefer + to exist, so the form has to be spelled correctly in either pattern.

takeaways: Used to + base verb is a past habit; be used to + gerund means accustomed now.
Adjectives with a fixed preposition always take the gerund: interested in, keen on.
Prefer doing compares general activities; prefer to do makes a specific choice.
When you see to after in, at, on or of, treat it as a preposition and use -ing.

lessons.title: The Gerund as a Subject
lessons.summary: When the -ing form works as the subject of a sentence, and what changes the meaning.

steps.heading: The Gerund as Subject and Object
steps.body: An -ing form can be the subject of a sentence, and then the verb that follows is singular because gerund subjects take a singular verb. The same -ing form can also be the object of a preposition, which is how a whole clause fits inside a phrase. These are the two positions where the gerund works as a noun, and they are the reason the form is called a gerund.

rules.title: Gerund as the subject
rules.statement: A gerund subject is singular and takes a singular verb. It is common with adjectives like important, dangerous, useless and interesting.

examples.en: Learning a language takes patience.
examples.vi: Học một ngôn ngữ cần sự kiên nhẫn.

examples.en: Waiting in line for an hour is exhausting.
examples.vi: Xếp hàng chờ một tiếng thật mệt.

rules.title: Gerund as the object of a preposition
rules.statement: The gerund can be the object of any preposition, which is how it fills the slot after in, on, of, for and about.

examples.en: I'm fond of cooking at home.
examples.vi: Tôi thích nấu ăn ở nhà.

examples.en: She is good at making people laugh.
examples.vi: Cô ấy giỏi khiến người ta cười.

rules.title: With versus without a preposition
rules.statement: Some verbs take a bare gerund and the same verb with a preposition takes a full clause. The preposition makes the structure heavier and more explanatory.
rules.formula: I insist on the fact that he was late. / I insist that he was late.

examples.en: He apologised for being late.
examples.vi: Anh ấy đã xin lỗi vì đến muộn.

examples.en: They objected to being interrupted.
examples.vi: Họ phản đối việc bị ngắt lời.

examples.en: Reading in dim light is bad for your eyes.
examples.vi: Đọc sách trong ánh sáng yếu có hại cho mắt.
examples.note: gerund subject with a singular verb

examples.en: I spent the afternoon sorting the files.
examples.vi: Tôi dành buổi chiều để sắp xếp hồ sơ.

examples.en: There's no point in arguing about it.
examples.vi: Tranh cãi về chuyện đó chẳng có ý nghĩa gì.

examples.en: She has a habit of biting her nails.
examples.vi: Cô ấy có thói quen cắn móng tay.

examples.en: Getting up early every day takes real motivation.
examples.vi: Dậy sớm mỗi ngày thật sự cần động lực.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.

items.text: Learning English takes a lot of time.
Learning English take a lot of time.
Learn English takes a lot of time.
Learning English are a lot of time.

exercises.explanation: A gerund subject is one thing, so the verb is singular: takes. Option b uses the plural verb, which is the error learners make when they mentally translate the gerund as an action with a doer rather than a single unit.

exercises.prompt: There's no point in ___ (worry) about something you cannot change.
exercises.explanation: The phrase no point in contains a preposition, and prepositions take the gerund: worrying. The same sentence with no point of would need a different construction entirely.

exercises.prompt: He apologised to be late for the meeting.

values: He apologised for being late for the meeting.

exercises.explanation: Apologise takes the preposition for, and after for the verb must be a gerund: for being late. To apologise is also wrong, because apologise is a verb of apology, not a verb of intention.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the correct order.
exercises.explanation: The phrase no point in is a fixed prepositional pattern, so the gerund worrying has to come directly after in, before the next preposition about. The word in therefore cannot be moved forward to join about, which is the trap this exercise sets.

audio.text: Studying a new subject requires a lot of discipline.

acceptedAnswers: Studying a new subject requires a lot of discipline.
items.translation: Học một môn mới đòi hỏi rất nhiều kỷ luật.

audio.text: I don't feel like cooking tonight.

acceptedAnswers: I don't feel like cooking tonight.
items.hint: like is followed by a gerund
items.translation: Tối nay tôi không muốn nấu ăn.

questions.prompt: Keeping a diary help a lot with learning.

values: Keeping a diary helps a lot with learning.

questions.explanation: The subject is the gerund phrase Keeping a diary, which counts as one thing, so the verb must be singular: helps. Using help would treat the gerund as a plural action.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a gerund correctly as the object of a preposition?

items.text: I'm fond of cooking traditional food.
I'm fond to cooking traditional food.
I'm fond of cook traditional food.

questions.explanation: Fond of is a prepositional phrase, so the gerund cooking follows the preposition. Option b replaces the preposition with an infinitive to, and option d puts a base verb after the preposition.

questions.prompt: Complete with the gerund: 'She avoided ___ the question directly.'
questions.explanation: Avoid is one of the gerund-only verbs, so answering is required. The gerund names the action that she steered clear of, which is why no to-infinitive is possible here.

takeaways: An -ing form can be the subject of a sentence, and then the verb is singular.
A gerund can be the object of any preposition: in, on, of, for, about, from.
There's no point in, I'm fond of and I don't feel like are all prepositional patterns.
Verbs like spend, mind, avoid and enjoy take a bare gerund with no preposition.

lessons.title: Noun Clauses and Advanced Patterns
lessons.summary: That-clauses, question clauses and the finer points of verb patterning.

steps.heading: Clauses that Fill a Noun Slot
steps.body: A clause can do the job of a noun, and in that case the verb pattern around it matters. Verbs of opinion, emotion and fact, such as think, know, believe and remember, take a that-clause in statement order. Verbs of saying and asking take a question clause with the normal question word order and no do or does. Getting the two apart is a reliable route to fluent complex sentences.

rules.title: That-clauses
rules.statement: Verbs of opinion, knowledge, emotion and fact are followed by a that-clause, which keeps statement word order.

examples.en: I think that she is right.
examples.vi: Tôi nghĩ cô ấy đúng.

examples.en: He admitted that he had been wrong.
examples.vi: Anh ấy thừa nhận rằng anh ấy đã sai.
examples.note: admit + that, the that may be omitted

rules.title: Question clauses after verbs of saying and asking
rules.statement: After ask, tell, wonder, know and similar verbs, the embedded question uses question word order but drops the auxiliary if there is one.
rules.formula: ask / wonder + whether / if / what / how + subject + verb

examples.en: She asked where the station was.
examples.vi: Cô ấy hỏi nhà ga ở đâu.
examples.note: no subject-auxiliary inversion: where the station was

examples.en: I wonder if they have finished.
examples.vi: Tôi tự hỏi họ đã xong chưa.
examples.note: the do is dropped: have, not do they have

rules.title: Verb patterns that differ in meaning
rules.statement: Some verbs change meaning with the clause type: a that-clause states a fact, while a gerund or infinitive clause presents the content as an idea or an intention.
rules.formula: I remember that I locked the door. / I remember locking the door. / I remember to lock the door.

examples.en: I believe that he is honest.
examples.vi: Tôi tin rằng anh ấy trung thực.

examples.en: He promised to return the money.
examples.vi: Anh ấy hứa sẽ trả lại khoản tiền.
examples.note: infinitive clause states a future intention

examples.en: Do you know when the library opens?
examples.vi: Bạn có biết thư viện mở cửa lúc nào không?
examples.note: embedded question: opens, not does it open

examples.en: He explained why the flight had been delayed.
examples.vi: Anh ấy giải thích lý do chuyến bay bị hoãn.

examples.en: I appreciate your taking the trouble to come.
examples.vi: Tôi trân trọng việc bạn đã cố gắng đến thăm.

examples.en: She admitted that she had taken the file.
examples.vi: Cô ấy thừa nhận đã lấy tệp tin đó.

examples.en: I'd rather you didn't mention the price.
examples.vi: Tôi thà bạn đừng nhắc đến mức giá.
examples.note: would rather + clause, not would rather you not to mention

exercises.prompt: She asked where was the meeting room.

values: She asked where the meeting room was.

exercises.explanation: Inside an embedded question the word order returns to statement order: where the meeting room was. The inversion of a direct question does not survive inside a that-less clause after a verb of asking.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.

items.text: I don't know what is his job.
I don't know what his job is.
I don't know what his job.
I don't know what is job his.

exercises.explanation: The embedded question keeps statement order, so the order is what his job is. Option a keeps the inversion of a direct question, and option c is simply an incomplete clause.

exercises.prompt: He suggested me to go to the hospital.

values: He suggested that I should go to the hospital.

exercises.explanation: Suggest cannot be followed by an object plus an infinitive, and it does not take a to-infinitive either. Two repairs are possible: the that-clause above, or the gerund form He suggested going to the hospital.

exercises.prompt: Which verbs are normally followed by a that-clause stating a belief or fact? Select all that apply.
exercises.explanation: Believe, know and suppose are verbs of opinion and fact, so they take a that-clause. Enjoy is an enjoyment verb and takes the gerund, not a clause.

exercises.prompt: Complete the clause: 'He admitted that he ___ the window before the storm.'
exercises.explanation: Inside a that-clause after admitted, the event reported is earlier than the admission itself, so the past perfect is required: had broken. Using broke would put the two events at the same time.

audio.text: I wonder whether we will finish the project on time.

acceptedAnswers: I wonder whether we will finish the project on time.
items.translation: Tôi tự hỏi liệu chúng ta có kịp hoàn thành dự án đúng hạn không.

audio.text: She insisted that he pay for the damage.

acceptedAnswers: She insisted that he pay for the damage.
items.hint: insist + that-clause with the bare form
items.translation: Cô ấy khẳng định rằng anh ấy phải bồi thường thiệt hại.

questions.prompt: Can you tell me where does the bus stop?

values: Can you tell me where the bus stops?

questions.explanation: After tell me the clause is embedded, so the word order is statement order: where the bus stops. The inversion of a direct question is only correct in a clause that is itself a question.

items.text: He admitted to take the money.
He admitted to taking the money.
He admitted that taking the money.

questions.explanation: Admit takes the gerund: admitted taking. Option b puts a base verb after a preposition, option c adds a to before the gerund, and option d leaves the clause without a verb.

questions.prompt: Write the -ing form of the verb 'to recommend'.
questions.explanation: Recommend doubles the d before -ing: recommending, because the stress is on the second syllable. The form appears in formal patterns such as I recommend booking early.

takeaways: Verbs of opinion, fact and emotion take a that-clause in statement order.
Verbs of asking take an embedded question with no auxiliary inversion.
Suggest and admit take the gerund; recommend and request take a noun plus a to-infinitive.
Inside a that-clause the tense normally shifts back one step, for example admitted that he had taken.
